video_title: How an American AI Company Uses Chinese Open-Weight Models | Odd Lots
gist: Minerva co-founder Daniel Saedi (ex-Bridgewater) explains how a US AI marketing startup uses frontier closed models to build product but fine-tunes Chinese open-weight models like Qwen and Kimi for cheap, repeatable production tasks, optimizing cost per completed task; the discussion covers fine-tuning economics (Harvey's ~$6M Tenant model, $7-9/M-token fine-tuning at Fireworks), data as the real moat, distillation debates, abliterated-model cyber risk, and a heuristic that the US is massively short compute (5-10M Blackwells vs ~100M knowledge workers).

insights.claim: Minerva uses frontier closed models (Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's models and others) to build its product because developer time is expensive, but for repeatable production tasks it optimizes cost per completed task rather than cost per million tokens.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: App-layer demand for frontier models skews to coding/building; production inference is price-sensitive and migrates to cheaper models.
insights.quote: you care about cost per completed task, which is a lot different than, you know, looking in the media where everyone cares about cost per million tokens

insights.claim: For an AI application company, margin is everything above the minimum acceptable task completion achieved at the lowest cost, so the goal is the cheapest model that clears the customer's quality bar.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Model choice at the app layer is a margin decision, not a capability race, which pressures premium token pricing.
insights.quote: how do I make sure that I get the minimum acceptable task completion for the lowest amount of costs? Because everything outside of that is our margin

insights.claim: Saedi ranks the benefits of open-weight models for US companies as: (1) cost, (2) data sovereignty/control, and (3) competitive leverage against single vendors.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Cost is the primary driver of open-weight adoption; sovereignty and vendor leverage are secondary but growing.
insights.quote: I think the most important thing is cost

insights.claim: The build-vs-buy equation is: per-token lab cost times number of tasks must exceed the upfront fine-tuning cost plus monthly operating cost of hosting the model for open weights to win, and it is true in many but not all cases.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Expect app-layer switching to be use-case-by-use-case rather than wholesale.

insights.claim: Harvey, which charges a fixed per-seat price, moved first to fine-tune its own legal model ('Tenant') because rising usage drove variable costs up against fixed revenue; usage-priced legal-tech rival 'Lagos' (as transcribed) is now exploring fine-tuning in response.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Seat-priced AI apps have the strongest incentive to defect from frontier APIs to protect operating margins.
insights.quote: Harvey has a per seat cost which is fixed and Lagos charges usage

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal frames the app-layer business model as selling a service at a recurring price while token prices fall ~90% per year, capturing the widening margin; Saedi confirms that is how Minerva and peers think about it.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Daniel Saedi
insights.so_what: Token price deflation accrues to application companies with fixed pricing rather than to model vendors.
insights.quote: that's exactly how I think us and other companies are thinking about it

insights.claim: Minerva's token budget has risen, not fallen, since the team moved fully to agentic coding around Opus 4.5 in October of last year, but it avoids 'token maxing' of $10-20K per engineer and aims for outcome-maxing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Even cost-conscious startups are increasing total AI spend as models improve; aggregate token demand keeps rising.
insights.quote: we're not spending like ten, 15, $20,000 per engineer for no token maxing

insights.claim: Even if open models win production workloads, many companies are still paying an 'Anthropic tax' or 'OpenAI tax', and public claims of using Chinese models (e.g. Coinbase's Brian Armstrong citing Kimi) can be posturing to gain pricing leverage.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Headlines about firms switching to open models may overstate actual frontier-lab revenue loss.
insights.quote: I think a lot of companies are paying an ant tax or an open AI tax

insights.claim: Tracy Alloway notes that privately, many large US companies admit to using Chinese models like Qwen, but not in public.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Chinese open-weight adoption in US enterprise is likely underreported.
insights.quote: A lot of them we'll talk about like Quinn and. Yeah, but not in public

themes.theme: Fine-tuning open weights as app-layer moat

insights.claim: Saedi argues fine-tuning open-weight models is the primary benefit to the application layer today, letting startups without the labs' billions in data specialize a general model on customer data.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: App companies with proprietary data can build differentiated, cheaper models, eroding frontier-lab pricing power on specific tasks.
insights.quote: this is the primary benefit to the application layer right now is the ability to fine tune on top of those openings

insights.claim: Minerva fine-tuned Qwen on a few thousand graded examples of complex audience queries (natural language to SQL), producing a model faster than closed models and better for its use case; out-of-the-box Qwen roughly matched an OpenAI model but trailed top frontier models.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: A few thousand labeled examples can be enough to beat frontier APIs on narrow tasks.
insights.quote: we have a few thousand of these labeled examples where you have a very complicated query

insights.claim: Application companies like Harvey and Cognition are fine-tuning Kimi on their proprietary data to match or beat frontier performance on customer tasks at lower cost, creating an advantage they can charge margin on.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Leading AI apps are building on Chinese open weights, a structural channel of Chinese model influence in US software.

insights.claim: Harvey reportedly spent about $6 million in compute to reach the frontier on legal tasks with its fine-tuned model, which Saedi says is 2-3 orders of magnitude off what frontier-model training/running costs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Domain-frontier performance is attainable for single-digit millions, a fraction of lab capex.
insights.quote: Harvey on their tenant model, spent about $6 million in compute

insights.claim: Fine-tunes do not transfer across model versions (e.g. Kimi 3 to Kimi 3.1); only the training dataset carries over, and because training recipes are undisclosed, re-convergence is uncertain, creating ongoing operational cost and risk.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Fine-tuning carries a recurring maintenance cost that must be priced into the build-vs-buy decision.
insights.quote: It doesn't simply transfer over

insights.claim: Open-weight competition gives smaller companies leverage to force the frontier labs into value-based pricing, since the alternative is no longer 'no automation' but a decent homegrown model.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Open-weight models cap frontier-lab pricing power with enterprise and app customers.
insights.quote: it gives the, the leverage back to, to the smaller companies

insights.claim: Saedi expects data sovereignty to be a huge issue in 2027 as companies realize they send data to Anthropic and OpenAI without the model improving for their use case, a point he attributes to Alex Karp and Satya Nadella.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Rising sovereignty concern favors fine-tunable open weights and enterprise self-hosting.
insights.quote: I imagine this is going to be a huge issue in 27

insights.claim: Open source and open weight are distinct: Chinese labs release model weights (the end artifact) for self-hosting, but not the training code, data and recipe.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Open-weight users remain dependent on opaque upstream training choices.

insights.claim: Fine-tuning and hosting have been commoditized over the past year by providers like Fireworks, Modal and Thinking Machines; previously it required a team of inference engineers, which is why few beyond research groups and large firms like Uber attempted it despite Llama being open for two years.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Lower barriers expand the addressable base of open-weight adopters.

insights.claim: Fireworks charges roughly $7-9 per million input and output tokens for fine-tuning, and some well-performing fine-tunes have cost as little as $90 for the final training run.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Fine-tuning cost has collapsed to near-trivial levels; data quality is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: I'm going to pay around 7 to $9 for per million input and million output tokens

insights.claim: Saedi says Fireworks and Modal are each at about $1 billion in annual revenue run rate with likely good unit economics, showing commoditization of a layer need not drive margins to zero.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Inference/fine-tuning platforms are a sizable, profitable layer benefiting from open-weight adoption.
insights.quote: both of them are sitting at $1 billion in error

insights.claim: DeepSeek recently published its entire inference framework, which Fireworks, Modal and others use to improve serving efficiency; Chinese labs also pioneered techniques like sparse models that save compute.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Chinese open research lowers serving costs industry-wide, pressuring inference pricing.

insights.claim: What separates a good fine-tune from a bad one is the data and evals, which is why labs pay data firms (transcribed as 'McCaw' and 'Serge') billions; the 'alpha' is in the data.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Expert data/eval vendors capture value as compute and fine-tuning commoditize.
insights.quote: the alpha per se is, as you would say, is in the data right now

insights.claim: Micro1, which Saedi calls the most legitimate company-data procurer, has paid $250-500K per complete company dataset and $50-100K just for referrals.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Corporate process data is a newly monetizable asset with steep market prices.
insights.quote: they're spending anywhere from 250 to 500 K per complete data set from a company

insights.claim: AI needs process data ('show your work'), not just outcomes: in construction, blueprints are available but the architect-contractor-client comments explaining changes are scarce, whereas marketing data (ads, call logs, website activity) is plentiful from the programmatic era.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Verticals with abundant process data (marketing) are automatable sooner than data-poor ones (construction).

insights.claim: Marketing data can be built into RL environments that simulate customer acquisition, e.g. testing whether an ad gets an AI agent to click through and buy.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: RL environments are becoming the unit of training data products.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal cites Google buying Spirit Airlines for $10 million for its corporate email and calendar data, and wonders whether zombie firms are worth more liquidated as training data.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Corporate data may create hidden asset value in distressed firms.
insights.quote: You got to wonder, how many zombie firms are out there that would be worth more if they just liquidated and sold all of their emails and corporate data to a lab?

themes.theme: Chinese open weights: distillation and the catch-up debate

insights.claim: Reflection AI, the leading US open-weight lab (allegedly being bought by Nvidia), trained its flagship on a 12-14K Blackwell cluster yet landed 3-6 months behind Chinese open models, which were themselves ~3 months behind the frontier; Saedi infers distillation is not the main reason Chinese labs are ahead.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Chinese labs' competitiveness reflects genuine research, so their open weights will likely keep pressuring US pricing.
insights.quote: it was probably about 3 to 6 months behind the Chinese open source models

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal pushes back that open-weight value may be subsidized by Chinese terms-of-service violations (distillation) that an American lab like the one behind Llama would not commit; Saedi agrees distillation is real and helps, citing the Kimi-Astra performance similarity, but says its share is debatable.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Daniel Saedi
insights.so_what: Regulatory or technical crackdowns on distillation are a risk to the open-weight cost advantage.
insights.quote: distillation is real, distillation is is real

insights.claim: Benchmarks are becoming meaningless; the real signal of Chinese models catching up is whether practitioners can swap Kimi in as their daily driver for coding and production workflows without degradation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Watch real-world substitution, not leaderboard scores, to judge commoditization of frontier intelligence.
insights.quote: the benchmarks are starting to become meaningless

insights.claim: The biggest risk of open-weight frontier models is 'abliteration': disabling refusal neurons in models like DeepSeek, yielding cheap uncensored models that can be used for hacking; online theory attributes current hacks to swarms of such models.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Cyber-risk is the most likely trigger for open-weight regulation (e.g. KYC for weight downloads), a key policy risk for the app layer.
insights.quote: people are running swarms of these deep seek obliterated models

insights.claim: An abliterated DeepSeek model costs about $0.30 per million blended tokens, roughly 10x cheaper than Sonnet, which is itself about 10x cheaper than the top frontier model, so roughly 1/100th the cost.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Near-frontier offensive capability is available at near-zero marginal cost.
insights.quote: It's about $0.30 per million or blended

insights.claim: Saedi says the labs' real concern with Chinese open weights is not data exfiltration to China but misuse via modified weights, and he suggests a middle ground such as KYC before downloading weights while preserving startup access.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Policy outcomes on open weights directly affect app-layer cost structures.
insights.quote: you have to KYC before you can download the weights

insights.claim: Saedi's first-principles heuristic: a fully AI-native knowledge worker needs about one GPU's worth of token consumption per year; with 5-10 million Blackwells deployed in the US versus ~100 million knowledge workers, the economy is massively short compute.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Supports a long-run bullish compute-demand thesis despite short-term overbuild narratives.
insights.quote: we're massively short of that need in the future

insights.claim: Saedi expects that roughly four years out there will be about one B300 worth of compute per knowledge worker, and that temporary overbuild narratives are noise around a long-term shortage.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Near-term GPU glut fears may be a buying opportunity for compute exposure.
insights.quote: in the long term we're still massively short the amount of compute we need

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal notes H100 rental price indices (Silicon Data) are still rising even amid AI-trade volatility, while Saedi reports compute for small fine-tuning jobs is readily available, unlike two years ago when H100s were unavailable.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Daniel Saedi
insights.so_what: Spot GPU pricing remains firm; scarcity concentrates at large-scale training rather than small fine-tunes.

insights.claim: Reports that Greg Brockman asked Elon Musk for compute while waiting for White House medals suggest frontier labs remain fundamentally short compute.
insights.speaker: Daniel Saedi (Minerva co-founder)
insights.so_what: Lab-level compute hunger persists.
insights.quote: Greg Brockman asked Elon for compute

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal cites an MIT research report where a frontier model (transcribed as 'Astor'/'after six') was fed Qwen's weights and directly edited them to improve math (fixing a bug), hinting at models improving models without traditional training.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: If models can edit weights directly, the highest-value use of frontier compute may be AI R&D itself.
